title: Intro to Computer Architecture
summary: How a computer is actually built and run — from the CPU cycle to why chips stopped getting faster every year.

blocks.markdown:
**Computer architecture** is the blueprint of a computer — what parts it has (CPU, memory, I/O) and how they're wired to run programs.

- It sits between software and physical hardware.
- Covers the **ISA** (the contract), the datapath, and how instructions actually run.
- Same ideas power a phone chip and a data-center server.

blocks.subTitle: Architecture vs organization vs microarchitecture
blocks.markdown:
People use these loosely, but they mean different layers.

- **Architecture (ISA)** — the programmer-visible contract: instructions, registers, memory model.
- **Organization** — how a design meets that contract: pipelines, cache sizes, bus widths.
- **Microarchitecture** — the specific chip implementation of the organization (e.g. one Intel generation vs another).

Same ISA, many organizations — that's how Intel and AMD both run x86.

Every computer, from a watch to a server, is built from the same four parts.

| Part | Job |
|---|---|
| CPU | Executes instructions |
| Memory | Holds running programs and data |
| I/O | Talks to the outside world (disk, network, screen) |

A **bus** is the shared wiring that moves data and addresses between them.

The **von Neumann model** (1945) stores instructions and data in the **same memory**, read over the **same bus**.

- Simple: one memory to design and manage.
- Bottleneck: CPU can't fetch an instruction and a data value at the same time — this is the **von Neumann bottleneck**.
- Nearly every general-purpose CPU today still follows it.

The **Harvard model** keeps instructions and data in **separate memories** with separate buses.

- Von Neumann: one memory — simpler, but fetch and data access compete.
- Harvard: two memories — instruction fetch and data access happen **at once**, faster.
- Cost: more wiring, and program size is capped by the fixed instruction memory.

Most CPUs today are a hybrid: von Neumann main memory, Harvard-style **split caches** for instructions and data.

blocks.subTitle: The fetch-decode-execute cycle
blocks.markdown:
Every instruction a CPU runs goes through the same three steps, on repeat.

<<< Image: a clean left-to-right cycle diagram, 3 nodes in a loop, blue/grey palette, generous whitespace. Nodes in order: 'Fetch', 'Decode', 'Execute'. Arrows connect Fetch to Decode to Execute and a curved arrow loops Execute back to Fetch. 1-2 word labels only. >>>

- **Fetch** — get the next instruction from memory, using the **program counter** (a register holding the next address).
- **Decode** — figure out what it means and which parts it needs.
- **Execute** — actually do it, then loop back to fetch.

blocks.subTitle: Why it matters
blocks.markdown:
This cycle is why clock speed matters: one **clock cycle** is roughly one tick of this loop.

- A 3 GHz chip aims for billions of these cycles per second.
- Real CPUs overlap cycles from different instructions (**pipelining**) instead of finishing one fully before starting the next.
- Pipelining is how modern chips run far faster than the raw cycle count suggests.

blocks.subTitle: The ISA as the contract
blocks.markdown:
The **ISA (instruction set architecture)** is the contract between software and hardware — the fixed list of instructions a CPU understands (add, load, jump, ...).

- Compilers target the ISA; they don't care how the chip implements it internally.
- Because the contract is fixed, Intel can redesign its chips every year and your old software still runs.
- Common ISAs: **x86** (desktops/servers), **ARM** (phones, Macs), **RISC-V** (open, growing fast).

Inside the CPU, two units do the real work.

- **ALU (arithmetic logic unit)** — does math and comparisons (add, subtract, AND, OR).
- **Control unit** — reads each instruction and steers the other parts (what to fetch, when to store).
- **Registers** — a handful of tiny, very fast storage slots inside the CPU, holding values mid-calculation.

Registers are far faster than memory, but there are only a few dozen of them.

Memory and I/O fill in the rest of the picture.

- **Memory** holds instructions and data while a program runs — RAM, plus faster **cache** layers closer to the CPU. Detailed in [memory-hierarchy](memory-hierarchy).
- **I/O (input/output)** connects the CPU to the outside world: keyboard, disk, network card, screen.
- The CPU talks to both over the **bus**, so a slow I/O device can hold up everything sharing that bus.

**Moore's law** (1965) observed that the number of transistors on a chip roughly **doubles every two years**.

- It's not physics — it's an economic/engineering trend that held for decades.
- More transistors meant faster, cheaper chips almost automatically, generation after generation.
- It shaped an entire industry's roadmap, not just one company's.

blocks.subTitle: Why it's slowing
blocks.markdown:
Moore's law is **slowing down** — transistors are hitting physical limits.

- Shrinking further runs into atomic-scale limits and heat that's hard to remove.
- Chipmakers now push performance sideways instead: more **cores**, specialized units (GPUs, AI accelerators), smarter software.
- This is why "just wait for faster chips" is a weaker strategy than it used to be.

Common mix-ups:

- **"Architecture and organization are the same thing."** No — architecture is the contract, organization is one way to meet it.
- **"Faster clock always means faster CPU."** Pipelining, cache misses, and instruction mix matter just as much.
- **"Moore's law is about speed."** It's about transistor count; speed gains were a side effect that's now fading.

blocks.subTitle: Von Neumann vs Harvard
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Von Neumann vs Harvard architecture — what's the difference?**

Von Neumann uses **one memory and bus** for both instructions and data, which is simple but creates a fetch bottleneck. Harvard uses **separate memories and buses**, so fetch and data access overlap.

Most real CPUs are hybrids: von Neumann main memory, Harvard-style split L1 caches for speed.

blocks.subTitle: The fetch-decode-execute cycle
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Walk me through the fetch-decode-execute cycle.**

The CPU **fetches** the next instruction using the program counter, **decodes** it to find the operation and operands, then **executes** it — and loops back to fetch the next one.

Every instruction any program runs goes through this loop; pipelining just overlaps the loops of successive instructions.

blocks.subTitle: What is an ISA
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is an ISA, and why does it matter?**

The **instruction set architecture** is the fixed set of instructions a CPU exposes to software — the contract between hardware and compilers/programs.

It matters because it lets hardware evolve underneath (new chip every year) while old compiled software keeps running unchanged.

blocks.subTitle: Architecture vs microarchitecture
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How is microarchitecture different from architecture?**

Architecture (the ISA) is what the programmer sees and never changes often. Microarchitecture is the actual chip design used to implement it — pipeline depth, cache sizes, branch prediction — and it changes every product generation.

Example: two Intel chip generations can share the same x86 ISA but have completely different microarchitectures.
